title: Ever virgin (CCC 499–501)
hookLine: Catholics and Orthodox hold that Mary remained a virgin; some Protestants read the brothers of Jesus differently

cards: Jesus comes back to his hometown and teaches in the synagogue, and the town can't get past who he is. Isn't this the carpenter? Isn't his mother called Mary?
Then they name names: his brothers, James and Joseph and Simon and Jude, and his sisters too, right here among us. Readers still stop at that line: brothers?
Today takes the second of yesterday's four teachings slowly, and that question with it. Today's word: ever virgin.

teach.b: The Catechism says Mary's virginity was real and lasting: before Jesus' birth, in it, and for the rest of her life. In the liturgy she's called ever virgin.
It starts with her question to the angel, in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?"
The Church reads her whole life as a yes given entirely to God, and her virginity as a sign of it: a heart, and a body, kept for the one who came to live in it. Then the brothers.
The Catechism answers the Nazareth line directly. James and Joseph, two of the names, are called elsewhere in Matthew the sons of another Mary, a disciple of Jesus.
The brothers and sisters, it says, are close relations of Jesus, in a way of speaking the Old Testament also uses, where relatives are called brothers.
Some early Christian writers thought they were Joseph's children from before he married Mary. Others thought they were cousins. And who reads what.

The Catholic and Orthodox churches both teach that Mary remained a virgin; the Orthodox call her ever-virgin in their prayers. Some Protestants read the brothers as later children of Mary and Joseph, and some do not.
Each reads the same pages carefully.
One more line from the Catechism: Jesus is Mary's only son, but her motherhood reaches out to everyone he came to save.
In Catholic teaching, ever virgin doesn't make her distant. It frees her to be mother to many.

how: Catholics call Mary ever virgin in the liturgy, including in the Confiteor at Mass, and the Orthodox call her ever-virgin in their prayers; the teaching is explained in the Catechism, paragraphs 496 to 501.

games.q: you're Mary. an angel says you'll bear a son. what do you say first?
o: an honest question: how shall this be done?
games.why: she asks, how shall this be done, because I know not man? the Church reads her question and her yes as one whole gift to God.

practice: Bring to mind one teaching, about Mary or anything else, that you find hard, or that people you love read differently, and don't argue it out; just hold it, the way Mary held the angel's words and asked, how shall this be done?
If you pray, ask for understanding, for yourself and for those who see it another way. If you don't, rest with the question, open.

wordCard.voice: Ever virgin. Mary's lasting virginity, before, during and after Jesus' birth, as Catholics and Orthodox teach it: a life given entirely to God.

orig.note: Greek: ever-virgin, the title used of Mary in Orthodox prayers.

carryVoice: Your line: ever virgin. An honest question is a good place to stand. I'll see you tomorrow.
